Name: Dennis Watson
Question: Do American people respect or love Muslim legal immigrants who obey American cultures at all?
Answer: I think in general, yes, but in my case, definitely yes. I grew up in a city with many immigrants from Islamic countries. Our nearby suburb, Dearborn, had the largest concentration of people from the Middle East in North America. I went to school with many muslims, I served with a few muslims, and my military unit had an interpreter who was muslim and was himself from Dearborn. I also had a doctor perform a life-saving surgery on me; that doctor was a muslim and wore a hijab. I thanked her profusely for the good work she did on me. (Islamic Center of America, in Dearborn, Michigan. Photo credit: Detroit Historical Society.) My favorite memories with muslim friends come from taking Tae Kwon Do at a martial art school in Dearborn and from my time working at a pizza parlor in a mostly Arab part of town. Most of my friends were from good, but stern homes. Many of their fathers ran their own businesses, while their mothers inevitably stayed home to attend to their children. I learned that my muslim friends suffered from the same problems non-muslims do. They think about sex, are tempted by alcohol, and drugs. Experience puberty, have silly notions about the world, use profanity, and a few were actually having sex. The image I previously had in my head of muslims being an extremely pious people was forever ruined. Needless to say, I think most immigrants from Islamic nations will adapt to American culture. If not in their own generation, their children’s generation.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How do you evaluate the Iraq War?
Answer: Poorly. In fact, we are still dealing with the repercussions of invading Iraq to this day. Not only that Iraq is an incredibly unstable country that has become an Iranian proxy. Not only that its economy has never flourished. Not only that it lead to the rise of ISIS and greater political instability throughout the region. What I mean, specifically, is the war in Ukraine. Putin, uses Iraq as an example as to how great powers actually don’t need to follow international law and that a rules-based order is just another myth used by the West when it is convenient to do so. In effect, might makes right. It’s impossible not to see hypocrisy in the actions of the United States when they call Russia out for invading a sovereign nation. The invasion of Iraq continues to handicap American foreign policy and calls into question the legitimacy of the West in enforcing a rules-based order. (Mural of Saddam Hussein near Baghdad International Airport. Photo by author.)

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: How long does it take people to stop hating everyone from a country they fought a war against?
Answer: To be clear, I never felt our fight was against the Iraqi people, but against the insurgency that had come to be by the time I was deployed to Iraq (2009). However, I could also clearly see that the insurgency was a direct result of American intervention in Iraq and that had it not been for our presence, they wouldn’t exist. The insurgents were also not all Iraqis. Some of them came from as far away as Chechnya for the opportunity to kill us. That said, I always thought the situation was a bit unfair. The insurgents could pull up alongside our base and lob rockets and mortars at us and then take off. They weren’t doing this because we were a direct threat to them, rather it seemed like a pastime they engaged in when they were bored on a Tuesday night. Their actions resulted in very real casualties and rarely were any of the perpetrators caught. The Iraqi military was mostly a pleasure to work with. Many of them had absolutely horrifying stories of death and survival that could not even be imagined by your average westerner. One guard from the Iraqi military managed to tell me in his broken English that his wife and kids had all been wiped out in a single bombing. He joined the military to get revenge. (Off duty in Baghdad. Photo by author.) That said, I never trusted anyone from the Iraqi military. I never turned my back on any of them when I had to work with them. Whenever I passed through an Iraqi military checkpoint I always unholstered my pistol and had it ready to fire. So to answer the question, I never hated any of the Iraqi people and never harbored any ill will towards anyone except for the insurgents that tried to kill us.

Name: Dennis Watson
Question: What are some unfair things about life?
Answer: A lot, perhaps even most things about life are unfair. Here are the most striking examples of unfairness in life: Youth are called on to make some of the most important decisions of their lives when they are young and very inexperienced. In most places, around the age of 18. College, military service, or entering the trades are all options. How can someone know if any of the above are for them before actually experiencing it? Choose wrong and you could spend multiple years correcting a mistake. Meanwhile, life still comes at you fast. The learning curve of life is steep! Life is expensive. Shockingly few people around the world are able to afford all the costs of daily living, yet people produce more value than at any other time in human history. There’s something inherently unfair about that. No Guarantees. You can do everything right in life and still end up in a shit situation. A friend of mine came from a difficult family and managed to go to college and dental school. Later she joined the Air Force and became an officer. Her life should have been good. However, she ended up in a relationship with another officer who abused hard drugs and gambled to excess. It nearly ruined her both personally and professionally. Time only goes forward. In life, there are no rewinds. That mistake you made 15 years ago not asking out your crush or passing up a job in that startup that is now worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Sorry, you’ll be living with that for the rest of your life. Where you’re born determines so much about your life. Even within developed countries this is true. Sometimes we can make predictions about someone’s life based on the very postal code in which they grew up. The person born in Libya will not have the same opportunities in life as the person born in Switzerland. Education is a key building block of life. Yet, our educational sysems are disparate in many, if not most parts of the world. The gap between elite schools and public schools is enormous, but we have high standards for all children, even if their education was insufficient. Health is vital to life and quality of life. Some people are born healthier than others. Modern medicine elliminates some, but not all disparities. There’s still much to be done in this area around the world.
